column3: Near-verbatim parallel: guidance has come, yet people withhold belief because they object to a human messenger.
The fading parable of worldly life gives only broad context for why people may defer response to guidance.
Unsupported idolatry does not materially clarify delayed belief, repentance, or punishment in the focus.
It asks whether they await angels or the Lord's command, explicitly linking their stance to the fate of earlier peoples.
The immediately preceding ayah says signs have been varied while the human response remains especially contentious.
Commands repentance and submission before punishment arrives, directly reversing the focus's fatal delay.
Their unbelief alongside the precedent of earlier peoples supports the focus's appeal to an established pattern.
Worldly adornment and enduring good deeds do not directly explain the focus's delayed faith and punishment.
Commands response before an irreversible day arrives, closely matching the focus's closing window for response.
Those facing punishment ask for delay so they can answer the call and follow messengers, making late repentance explicit.
The immediate continuation shows disbelievers disputing truth and mocking the warnings they have received.
A question about a missing object has no material relation to the focus.
Faith adopted only when decisive signs arrive no longer benefits, directly paralleling response deferred until compulsion.
The gathering of all people on the Last Day is a distant consequence of refusing the guidance now offered.
The crowd rushing toward Abraham does not clarify the focus's warning.
It challenges people who have not reflected on the message and treat it as unprecedented, a secondary form of resistance to guidance.
The denied appointment is realized when people stand before their Lord, supplying the eventual outcome of the focus's delay.
They repeatedly turn away whenever a sign of their Lord comes, describing the reception failure behind delayed belief.
Disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour suddenly comes or a barren-day punishment reaches them.
The complete record of deeds and the criminals' alarm give a judgment context for refusing guidance and repentance.
The expiation rule for zihar does not provide a neighbour relation to the focus.
It warns that evildoers cannot be secure from punishment arriving unexpectedly, a related threat though without the focus's guidance sequence.
Iblis's disobedience and false patronage are not needed to clarify the focus's delayed response.
Having received and forgotten divine signs leads to being forgotten, reinforcing culpable disregard of guidance.
Earlier peoples denied warning signs, and signs are sent as warnings, directly supporting the focus's reference to their precedent.
The lack of witness to creation does not clarify delayed faith or punishment.
The challenge to produce alleged partners is not a material neighbour of the focus.
Even overwhelming, face-to-face evidence would not make them believe, exposing that the obstacle is not lack of guidance.
At judgment the alleged partners cannot answer and a destructive barrier stands between them, a secondary outcome parallel.
The introduction to Moses's story has no relevant connection.
Desire for prolonged life cannot move a person away from punishment, a remote counterpart to delaying response.
Criminals see the Fire, know they will enter it, and find no escape, depicting the finality anticipated by the focus.
The gift of scripture for guidance is only a general parallel to the guidance that has come in the focus.
They turn away whenever a sign of their Lord comes, closely echoing the focus's failure to believe after guidance arrives.
The immediate next ayah condemns turning from recalled signs and records the barriers that follow such refusal.
Divine guidance is sent and following it removes fear and grief, supplying the positive alternative to the focus's refusal.
Guidance has come from the Lord, yet people follow conjecture and desire instead, directly explaining rejection despite guidance.
The Merciful Lord does not hasten punishment, but has fixed an appointment from which there is no refuge.
Demanding angels as proof is dangerous because their coming would close the period of testing rather than merely add evidence.
Ending disbelief brings forgiveness, while persistence invokes the established precedent of earlier peoples.
Destroyed towns were given an appointed time for their destruction after wrongdoing, directly illustrating the focus's former-peoples precedent.
Those in punishment are reminded that messengers came with clear proofs, making their later plea futile.
Persecution because believers have faith supplies only distant background on opposition to belief.
The testing of Pharaoh's people by a noble messenger is a limited historical example of guidance coming to a community.
They deny truth when it comes, and the news they mocked will come to them as realized consequence.
Social hostility from some People of the Book does not clarify the focus's warning.
God does not punish them while they seek forgiveness, directly relating repentance to the withholding of punishment.
The arrival of certainty marks the closure of the period in which conduct and response could still change.
Noah's call to seek the Lord's forgiveness gives the immediate remedy the focus says people postpone.
Competing in good deeds and differing directions do not materially clarify the focus.
Every messenger who came to them was mocked, a recurring response pattern behind the focus's warning.
The claim of being approached from the right has no material relation to the focus.
They cannot understand, refuse belief even after every sign, and dispute by calling the message ancient tales.
Noah's people as transgressors provides only a bare historical predecessor.
The arrogant acknowledge that guidance came to the weak, who nevertheless became guilty, stressing responsibility after guidance.
Moses being called at the fire does not clarify the focus.
God's unchanged practice among those who passed before anchors the focus's reference to the precedent of earlier peoples.
Their demand to hasten their allotted judgment before the Day of Account parallels the reckless demand for punishment.
The Prophet's grief over their refusal to believe gives immediate narrative context for the focus's diagnosis of that refusal.
The demand for direct speech or a new sign repeats the speech of earlier peoples despite signs already made clear.
Wrongdoers will recognize all power belongs to God when they see punishment, an outcome-related parallel to the focus.
Truth has come to them, yet they are liars, concisely matching the focus's premise that guidance has already arrived.
God's unchanging established practice reinforces the focus's warning about the precedent of the earlier peoples.
Lot's people answer moral rebuke by demanding God's punishment, a direct parallel to defiant postponement until punishment.
Clear signs brought by Moses are dismissed as fabricated magic and rejected because they were unknown to the ancestors.
Joseph's interpretation of provisions and his personal history do not clarify the focus.
The contrast between belief leading to forgiveness and idolatry leading to Fire is only a broad moral parallel.
Prior luxury alone does not establish a material neighbour relation to the focus.
The unchanging precedent governing messengers supports the focus's appeal to the established fate of earlier communities.
God's appointed meeting is certainly coming, supplying a general temporal certainty beside the focus's coming punishment.
The Quran as guidance and clear criteria is a general, but not specific, parallel to guidance arriving in the focus.
The listing of earlier deniers supplies historical background for the focus's reference to former peoples.
Preventing remembrance in mosques is not a material neighbour of the focus.
Belief in revelation and the Hereafter gives only a broad positive contrast to the focus's unbelief.
At standing before their Lord, disbelievers finally affirm the truth and are told to taste punishment for their disbelief.
A sound heart is not a distinct clarification of delayed belief, repentance, or punishment here.
The community's former weakness and rescue are not a material neighbour of the focus.
Selective rejection of later revelation is a secondary example of refusing truth after it arrives.
The withholding of a grain measure has no relevant relation to the focus.
Belief before death presents a final temporal boundary, but concerns a different claim and audience.
Ritual limits and social conduct do not clarify the focus.
After denying, the news they mocked will come to them, turning rejected warning into realized consequence.
The magicians' hope for forgiveness after faith is a general repentance resonance only.
The historical recurrence of messengers being denied is relevant but too general to clarify the focus's specific sequence.
The description of unwithheld fruit has no relation to the focus.
No prophet came to them without their mocking him, a recurrent rejection pattern for revealed warning.
It warns against a covering punishment or the sudden Hour arriving while they are unaware.
They demand a sign despite the proof already having come in earlier scriptures, closely matching refusal after guidance.
Persistent disbelief can make even repeated requests for forgiveness ineffective, an endpoint-related contrast to timely repentance.
Universal servitude to the Most Merciful does not clarify the focus's warning.
Universal praise and human failure to understand it are not a material neighbour relation.
Every messenger is met with mockery, depicting the repeated waste of opportunities to heed warning.
When people sense divine punishment they flee, illustrating the late, futile reaction anticipated by the focus.
The report of Abraham's guests is not relevant to delayed belief or punishment.
Its commands to seek forgiveness and heed revelation give only broad devotional support.
The description of untouched companions has no relation to the focus.
Self-sufficiency may underlie refusal of guidance, but the ayah is too indirect to be a strong neighbour.
The creation of jinn before humanity does not clarify the focus.
Cosmic governance and powerless idols are not a material neighbour of the focus.
The brothers' accusation and Joseph's restraint have no relation to the focus.
After they forgot the warning, they were seized suddenly amid worldly ease, illustrating delayed response ending in abrupt punishment.
It asks whether sudden or open punishment destroys anyone but the wrongdoing people.
Some refuse to believe until granted a sign like that given to messengers, a direct instance of conditional belief after guidance.
Communities receiving a prophet are tested with hardship so that they might humble themselves, supplying an earlier-peoples warning pattern.
After dismissing hardship as ancestral fluctuation, a people are seized suddenly while unaware.
Past destroyed communities warn later inheritors that God can strike people for their sins and seal their hearts.
Messengers brought clear proofs to earlier towns, but they would not believe what they had denied before.
The disbelievers demand that, if the message is true, punishment be sent upon them, a close parallel to defiant postponement.
The people of Pharaoh and those before them disbelieved in God's signs, so God seized them for their sins.
It repeats the Pharaoh precedent: denial of signs brings destruction for wrongdoing.
Earlier generations were destroyed after their messengers brought clear proofs and they would not believe.
Those against whom the Lord's word is realized will not believe.
Even every sign will not avail them until they see the painful punishment.
Jonah's people are the exceptional case whose timely belief removed the punishment of disgrace.
It asks whether they await anything except days like those of earlier people who passed away.
When punishment is deferred to an appointed term, deniers ask what holds it back, and its arrival cannot be turned away.
People hasten evil before good although exemplary punishments have already passed before them.
Disbelievers continue to be struck by calamity or have it strike near them until God's promise comes.
The message about Noah, Ad, Thamud, and later peoples recalls earlier communities who rejected their messengers.
Wrongdoers are reprieved only to an appointed term that they cannot delay or advance.
When wrongdoers see the Fire, neither mitigation nor reprieve remains available.
Seeing punishment does not secure delay or a chance to make amends.
Their punishment follows disbelief in the signs and denial of resurrection, reinforcing the judgment consequence of refusing guidance.
It records the excuse that, had destruction come first, people would have asked for a messenger and followed the signs.
Many wrongdoing towns were shattered and replaced, an explicit historical punishment precedent.
The promised punishment will come suddenly, bewildering those who had mocked it.
When the affluent are seized with punishment, they cry out, but are told they will not be helped.
Even when mercy removes affliction, they persist in rebellion and wander blindly.
When severe punishment is opened upon them, they fall into despair.
Noah's people denied the messengers and were drowned, made a sign, and assigned painful punishment.
They ask you to hasten punishment, though Hell already encompasses the disbelievers.
The evil end belongs to those who denied God's signs and mocked them.
Those who forgot the meeting of this Day are told to taste the abiding punishment.
The lesser punishment is made to precede the greater so that they might return.
None is more unjust than one reminded of the Lord's signs who then turns away.
Earlier peoples denied, and the later deniers have not reached a fraction of their strength, yet they too reject the messengers.
Those before them denied, and God's repudiation came upon them.
Those before them denied, then punishment came from where they did not perceive.
It commands following the best revealed before punishment comes suddenly while people are unaware.
It depicts regret for neglecting duty toward God after the opportunity has passed.
It records the excuse that guidance would have produced greater piety, showing the lost opportunity to respond.
On seeing punishment, the wrongdoer wishes for another return to act rightly.
God answers that His signs had already come, but were denied in arrogance.
Earlier nations plotted against their messenger and disputed to defeat truth, so each was seized.
Earlier peoples were stronger and left greater traces, yet God seized them for their sins.
When messengers came with clear proofs, people exulted in their own knowledge and were encompassed by what they mocked.
When they saw God's punishment, they professed belief, a direct late-belief parallel.
Faith at the sight of punishment did not benefit them under God's established practice for His servants.
Turning away from revelation brings warning of a thunderbolt like that of Ad and Thamud.
A humiliating punishment was sent upon Ad in worldly life, with the Hereafter still more disgraceful.
People persist in inherited ways even when a messenger brings guidance better than what they found their forefathers following.
God took retribution from those who denied, directing attention to the outcome of deniers.
A people mistake the approaching punishment for a rain cloud, then it destroys all by its Lord's command.
Traveling the land displays the end of those before who denied, an explicit historical-warning parallel.
Knowledge of the promised time belongs to God, while the messenger's task is only clear warning.
When the promised punishment is seen near, the faces of disbelievers darken and they are confronted with what they sought to hasten.
When the promised warning is seen, opponents will know who is weaker in helper and number.
It challenges those who await only God's command and angels in overshadowing clouds, when every matter returns to God.
The People of the Book demand to see God openly, recalling an earlier demand that was met with a thunderbolt for wrongdoing.
The demand for an angel is answered by saying that, if one were sent, the matter would be decided and no respite remain.
Earlier messengers were mocked, and the mockers were encompassed by what they derided.
Earlier communities were sent adversity and hardship so that they might humble themselves.
When hardship came, they did not humble themselves; their hearts hardened and Satan made their deeds fair to them.
It warns of punishment sent from above, below, or through factional conflict, a broad punishment parallel.
Humankind and jinn are asked whether messengers recited the signs and warned them of meeting this Day.
God does not destroy towns for wrongdoing while their people are unaware, establishing warning before punishment.
Many towns were destroyed when punishment came by night or while their people rested at midday.
When punishment came, the destroyed people's only cry was admission that they had been wrongdoers.
Pharaoh's people were afflicted with years of scarcity and loss of crops so that they might remember.
Pharaoh's people declare that no sign will make them believe, an explicit statement of resistant reception.
Successive plagues are sent as distinct signs, yet Pharaoh's people persist in arrogance and crime.
When punishment falls, Pharaoh's people promise belief and release if it is removed.
Once punishment is removed to its term, Pharaoh's people break their promise.
It asks what part of God's punishment criminals are trying to hasten, whether it comes by night or day.
It rebukes belief only after punishment has occurred, when people had sought to hasten it.
Wrongdoers are told to taste the abiding punishment as recompense for what they earned.
The Lord's seizure of wrongdoing towns is painful and severe.
The Lord would not destroy towns unjustly while their people were reforming.
Messengers before were mocked, then disbelievers were given respite before being seized.
Disbelieving peoples threaten to expel messengers, and revelation answers that the wrongdoers will be destroyed.
The messengers seek victory, and every stubborn tyrant is disappointed.
Angels descend only with truth, and when they come the deniers are not reprieved.
Those before plotted, then God's punishment came from where they did not perceive and their structure collapsed upon them.
No punishment is imposed until a messenger has been sent, defining the warning that precedes accountability.
Many generations after Noah were destroyed, and God is fully aware of His servants' sins.
Every town is either destroyed or severely punished before the Day of Resurrection, by a decree recorded in the Book.
Those prolonged in error will eventually see the promised punishment or the Hour and know whose position is worse.
The destruction of many earlier generations whose dwellings remain is presented as a sign for people of understanding.
No town destroyed before them believed after seeing the signs, challenging the expectation that these deniers will believe.
Noah, Ad, Thamud, Abraham's people, Lot's people, and Midian all denied, placing the focus in a broad historical pattern.
God gave deniers respite and then seized them, showing the consequence of rejecting messengers.
The people of Hell are asked whether the Lord's signs had been recited to them and were then denied.
Moses and Aaron are told to go to a people who denied the signs, after which those people are destroyed.
The destruction and deliverance in the Moses narrative are a sign, though most people do not believe.
Deniers do not believe until they see the painful punishment.
The punishment comes upon them suddenly while they are unaware.
It rebukes those who ask for God's punishment to be hastened.
After a calamity, people would claim that a messenger should have been sent so they could follow the signs and believe.
Many towns exulting in prosperity were destroyed, leaving their dwellings scarcely inhabited afterward.
The Lord does not destroy towns until He sends a messenger to recite His signs in their central community.
Each prior community was seized for its sin by a fitting punishment, and God did not wrong them.
Travel through the land reveals the end of those before, who were stronger and more productive but were overtaken after messengers came with clear proofs.
People swear that if a warner comes they will be better guided, but the warner's arrival only increases their flight.
Their arrogance and plotting are met by the unchanging practice applied to earlier peoples.
The Quran warns a people whose forefathers were not warned and who are heedless.
The word has become due against most of them, so they do not believe.
Deniers ask when the promise will come if the warning is true.
They await only one blast that will seize them while they are disputing.
Those raised from graves recognize that this is what the Most Merciful promised and the messengers declared true.
Those who deny the Book and the message sent through the messengers are warned that they will come to know.
Many prophets were sent among earlier peoples, establishing the long history of repeated warning.
God destroyed peoples stronger than the later deniers, while their earlier example has already passed.
Nearby towns were destroyed after signs were varied for them so that they might return.
The Day they see what they were promised, the time they spent will seem only an hour of a day.
The people of the thicket and Tubba's people also denied messengers, and God's threat was fulfilled.
Hell nearly bursts with rage, and each group cast into it is asked whether a warner had not come.
They admit that a warner came, but they denied him and rejected the revelation.
A questioner asks for the punishment that will inevitably fall upon the disbelievers.
